Stable plasma ignition and operation were consistently achieved for flow rates up to approximately 300 SLPM. Above this threshold, the plasma exhibited intermittent discharge behavior attributed to reduced residence time and increased gas velocity. Beyond 500 SLPM, plasma ignition could not be sustained, establishing the upper limit of stable operation for the prototype geometry. Electrical performance was monitored using real-time voltage and current traces to confirm proper energy coupling between the pulse-power system and the plasma discharge. Figure 13 compares oscilloscope waveforms recorded during plasma-off and plasma- on conditions. The reflection peaks visible in the plasma-off trace disappeared when the plasma was active, indicating a substantial impedance change due to energy absorption by the ionized gas. This behavior confirmed stable discharge formation and validated when the electrical energy was being transferred into the plasma rather than reflected back to the power supply. Figure 13 intentionally omitted from public version. Electrical diagnostics conducted during high-flow testing confirmed a clear distinction between plasma-off and plasma-on operating conditions. When the plasma was inactive, electrical measurements indicated inefficient energy coupling between the power system and the reformer. Upon plasma ignition, the electrical response changed in a manner consistent with effective energy absorption by the plasma discharge, indicating stable plasma formation. The left image (plasma off) shows multiple voltage reflection peaks caused by impedance mismatch, while the right image (plasma on) shows the disappearance of these peaks as the plasma forms and absorbs the applied energy. However, at the higher flow rate conditions the mass spectrometer system was not able to maintain a sufficiently low pressure in the detector to collect reliable data. Plasma stability was verified through repeated ignition cycles, demonstrating the reformer’s ability to maintain a uniform discharge under dynamic flow conditions representative of engine operation. Post-test inspection of the plasma reformer revealed visible carbon deposition on the inner surfaces of the reactor walls, confirming that methane decomposition had occurred similar to bench-scale testing. The carbon deposits were again loosely adhered and easily removed using a solvent wipe. Figure 14 shows the interior of the reformer following high-flow operation, where black carbon residue is visible on the cloth wipe. The reduced quantity of deposited carbon suggests that the majority of solid carbon was transported downstream by the high velocity gas stream before adhering to the reactor wall, which should minimize the risk of long-term fouling on the electrode.
